title: This Oil Company Is Linked to 1,000 Pollution Incidents and Other Violations. Oklahoma Never Punished It.
author: Nick Bowlin
content:
In June 2023, staff at an Oklahoma regulatory agency were fed up. The state
isn’t known for cracking down on oil and gas companies for polluting the
environment, but for over a year, the staff had been building a case to punish
Citation Oil & Gas, one of the nation’s largest privately owned oil companies.

About 30 miles north of the Texas border, toxic wastewater was gushing from
the ground outside the small city of Ardmore. In the mile-wide oil field known
as the Bayou, an oily sheen glistened on creeks and long streaks of salt
scarred the land. The so-called purges, bubbling up among stands of oak and
walnut trees, also threatened drinking water sources, drawing attention from
the Environmental Protection Agency, according to a federal report.

State investigators pinned the blame on Citation’s injection wells, which pump
wastewater from oil production back underground at high pressures and volumes
in order to produce more oil. But this injection came with risks.

Days earlier, the agency had asked Citation to cut injection pressures in
half. The company refused, prompting staff at the oil division of the Oklahoma
Corporation Commission, the state’s oil and gas regulator, to recommend an
official punishment through the agency’s court system.

“This will be an important case to get some of these purges stopped and
particularly concerning Citation’s operations,” Danny Ray, an agency manager
at the time, emailed his colleagues.

He restated the urgency three days later in an email to oil division leaders
and Citation officials: “We consider this an emergency situation that needs to
be addressed promptly.”

old well releases a stream of wastewater in the Bayou in 2022. Obtained in an

To stop the flow of wastewater, the agency temporarily shut down the Bayou’s
22 injection wells — all but three of which were owned by Citation — kicking
off a yearlong fight over the terms under which injection could restart.

Under state rules, companies must not pollute, and oil and gas regulators at
the Corporation Commission can revoke injection permits and issue fines to
those that violate regulations.

But agency leadership ultimately did not follow staff guidance to punish
Citation through the commission’s administrative law court. Instead, in April
2024, state officials, including the oil division’s then-Director Robyn
Strickland, would allow Citation to restart injection at higher-than-
recommended pressures.

Agency leaders’ reluctance to punish Citation reflects a longstanding pattern
of Oklahoma regulators letting oil companies [contaminate drinking
water](https://www.propublica.org/article/oklahoma-oil-polluted-drinking-
water-boarman-family), [farmland](https://www.propublica.org/article/oklahoma-
oil-gas-wastewater-pollution) and [people’s
homes](https://www.propublica.org/article/oklahoma-oil-regulators-fort-gibson-
meredith-family) with scant consequences, The Frontier and ProPublica have
found in a [yearlong investigation](https://www.propublica.org/series/toxic-
pressure).

In fact the commission has no record of ever fining or completing an
enforcement case against Citation, the company named more than any other in
the [agency’s database of pollution
reports](https://gis.occ.ok.gov/portal/apps/experiencebuilder/experience/?id=75bcb0b2c7f943dfa6cec75a50c9205a)
and other rule violations, listed more than 1,000 times over the past decade.
That’s hundreds more incidents than any other operator, including comparably
sized companies. In recent years, purges linked to Citation include some of
Oklahoma’s longest, most damaging oil field pollution events.

Current and former employees at the Oklahoma Corporation Commission describe
top agency officials as wary of going after habitual violators like Citation.
Citation has become Oklahoma’s second-largest well owner after taking over
collections of aging, low-producing wells from oil giants that have largely
left the state for more lucrative oil fields in Texas and elsewhere; the
company acquired its Bayou wells in 2010. Regulators treat Citation gently,
current and former agency employees say, because the company holds onto aging
wells that are worth little — wells that could easily become a financial
liability for the state if Citation were to sell or walk away from them.

A spokesperson for the Oklahoma Corporation Commission declined to answer
questions about the regulatory agency’s handling of Citation’s record, noting
the possibility of future enforcement actions or litigation involving the
company.

“The OCC Oil and Gas Conservation Division must remain mindful of its
regulatory and adjudicatory responsibilities and avoid making public
statements that could potentially affect future proceedings or legal
considerations,” spokesperson Jack Damrill said in an email.

Strickland has since left the agency for a job as chief projects officer for
the[ Interstate Oil and Gas Compact
Commission](https://www.propublica.org/article/oil-industry-lobbying-
unplugged-wells), a quasi-governmental organization that often advocates for
industry interests. She did not respond to requests for comment.

A Citation executive declined to comment in response to written questions.

Regulators in other jurisdictions have at times [come down
hard](https://violationtracker.goodjobsfirst.org/parent/citation-oil-and-
gas#:~:text=%24208%2C250.%20Citation%20Oil%20%26%20Gas%20Corp.%20oil,Corporation.%20wage%20and%20hour%20violation.%202020.%20WHD)
on Citation, which owns wells in 11 other states. In 2017, the company
[settled with the U.S. Department of
Justice](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/citation-companies-agree-
pay-225-million-settle-civil-false-claims-act-allegations) for $2.25 million
over allegations of underpaid royalties from drilling on federal land in
Wyoming, though the settlement did not rule that the company was liable in the
case. And in 2025, Utah reached a [$700,000
settlement](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/when-citation-oil-and-gass-
pipeline-broke-share-7467606038226321408-LJBx/) with the company after a crude
oil and wastewater spill. Texas and Colorado have also fined Citation in
recent years for violations.

“Citation has been the thorn in my side for a long time,” said a current
manager at the Oklahoma agency who spoke on the condition of anonymity to
protect their job. “They just operate however they want. They've had major
pollution issues, and you can’t really touch them.”

![Signage for Citation Oil & Gas on a fence in front of a field with an oil
well.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261007-Oxford-
Oklahoma-
Citation-007_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)A
Citation Oil & Gas oil well in the Bayou. The company is named more often than
any other in Oklahoma’s database of oil field pollution incidents and other
rule violations. Nick Oxford for ProPublica

### Preparing a Case for Punishment

In November 2023, five months into the wells’ shutdown, Citation was getting
antsy. Its officials had repeatedly demanded permission to restart their wells
and had even challenged the state through the commission’s court to prove the
connection between the Bayou purges and its operations. Regulators and company
officials packed into a small conference room in the Oklahoma Corporation
Commission’s Oklahoma City headquarters to discuss how that might happen. More
than a dozen others joined via video.

On the state’s side, a team of consultants took the lead, displaying a report
with evidence that tied Citation’s injection to the wastewater that gushed to
the surface in the Bayou. The state had hired the environmental engineering
firm Halff earlier that year on a $550,000 contract to investigate the fast-
growing number of oil field wastewater eruptions around Oklahoma. The
consultants and agency staff presented a unified front in identifying the
problem: Citation’s nearly two dozen Bayou injection wells were operating at
unsafely high pressures, according to a video recording of the meeting
obtained by The Frontier and ProPublica. Over the years, the injected
wastewater had shattered underground rock layers, allowing the toxic fluid to
spread uncontrollably.

“You definitely have overpressurization,” Carolyn May, Halff’s director of
environmental remediation, told Citation officials as she presented her team’s
calculations, which were based on well records, field data collected by agency
staff and a standard set by the federal government. “It's allowing that rock
to fracture.”

The consultants were meant to serve as independent experts to mediate any
disagreements within the agency over what to do about the wastewater
eruptions, according to current and former commission officials.

In the meeting, May and agency staffers ticked off a number of problems with
Citation’s wells that regulators had overlooked for years. Not only had they
allowed the company to inject wastewater at excessive pressures, regulators
had also given out more than a dozen exemptions to testing and well-
construction standards that endangered groundwater. Several wells had
checkered compliance records; agency documents noted that one had been in
“perpetual violation” of its permit for “nine years running,” injecting tens
of millions of gallons of wastewater beyond the legal limit.

Citation’s active wells weren’t the only issue, they said. Nearby were dozens
of abandoned, unplugged wells that offered the pressurized wastewater open
pathways to reach shallow freshwater sources and the surface. May singled out
a handful of those wells that especially troubled her team, and oil division
deputy director Mike McGinnis suggested that Citation permanently plug them.

May noted that imaging below the surface by agency staff showed a distinct
plume of highly polluted wastewater rising from deep underground, where
injection took place. This posed a threat to the freshwater sources beneath
the Bayou, she said — water that some residents rely on for drinking and
cooking. “That’s our primary concern here.”

The consultants were not alone in this fear. Earlier in 2023, the
Environmental Protection Agency had warned of "potential endangerment to
underground sources of drinking water" in the Bayou from oil field injection.
Groundwater tests taken near the purge sites showed evidence of oil field
wastewater pollution, including high levels of salt, bromide and the
carcinogen benzene, which exceeded the EPA drinking water standard by five
times.

For its part, Citation came to the meeting armed with a very different
argument: the pollution was caused by a combination of historic oil drilling
and recent rainfall — not by the company.

It was a claim the company had repeatedly made, especially in the months since
the agency had shut down its wells. To bolster its case, the company’s
consultants had produced a series of detailed reports citing the area’s
history of oil production, along with Citation’s own water testing data. Oil
drilling began in the Bayou in the 1920s, a time of lawless extraction, and
for decades, companies would simply dump their wastewater into large, unlined
pits, allowing the fluid to seep into the ground. Old pollution that saturated
the land was being flushed to the surface by rainfall, the reports argued.
Each one concluded that there was no link between Citation’s injection and the
Bayou pollution.

At the meeting with regulators, company representatives reiterated these
arguments. Jeff Lewis, a Citation engineering manager, assured the agency that
the company’s data indicated that its wells were not behind the Bayou purges
and that it could safely inject at pressures higher than Halff had
recommended. He proposed that the company restart injection on its deeper
wells because they were separated by layers of rock from the abandoned wells
that Halff identified as likely pathways for the wastewater to surface.

Agency staff did not buy this. In prior internal meetings and emails, staff
and consultants had criticized Citation’s water sampling practices as biased
in favor of the company’s conclusion that rainfall was causing old pollution
to resurface. There was no question that old pollution covered the Bayou, but
in recent purges, wastewater had pushed to the surface in significant volumes,
covering creek beds in layers of snow-white salt. Old pollution would not be
this forceful, according to internal documents written by agency staff.

"A purge is created by pressure and is not due to old pits,” Ray, the agency
manager, wrote in a memo distributed months earlier within the oil division
that urged agency leaders not to allow Citation to restart injection.

May, the agency’s consultant, echoed these rebuttals during the meeting and
said the state’s evidence pointed to an injection problem. She concluded her
presentation with a warning: Citation must change its injection practices in
the Bayou.

“If y'all want to start injecting again,” she told company representatives, “I
think we're going to have to look at those pressures and the volumes very
carefully.”

The meeting ended without a resolution.

### “They Wore Us Out”

Over the next four months, Citation and state regulators would continue to
debate the terms of restarting the Bayou. Neither side budged. By the time
they gathered for another face-off in March 2024, oil division leaders
appeared weary of fighting.

May and the Halff geologists from the consulting firm began by again insisting
that Citation substantially reduce pressures in order to be allowed to restart
a handful of wells. But even as they presented their case, Citation
representatives including Lewis, the engineer, and Bob Redweik, a company vice
president, repeatedly spoke over them. After more than two hours of
disagreement, Redweik and Citation’s attorney ended the meeting abruptly.
“We’re not going anywhere,” Redweik said.  

Several top oil division officials attended, including Strickland, McGinnis
and commission attorney Tyler Trout. They remained largely silent throughout.

The next week, Trout tried to end the impasse by passing along a memo from
Citation.

“In an effort to reach an agreement and move this situation forward,” Trout
wrote to top oil division officials and May, “would we consider meeting
Citation in the middle as far as recommended injection pressures are
concerned?”

May stood firm. “From Halff’s standpoint, our recommendations aren’t going to
change,” she responded, adding that it would ultimately be up to agency
leaders.

In early April, the agency went with a compromise, approving a plan to bring
seven of Citation’s 19 Bayou injection wells back online. The company would be
able to inject at pressures higher than Halff had recommended, though less
than Citation had requested.

Current and former employees say that the decision to restart injection came
from the top of the oil division, including Strickland and McGinnis, among
others — bypassing staff who objected to the plan. Like Strickland, McGinnis
did not respond to requests for comment.

“They wore us out,” said an agency manager who spoke on the condition of
anonymity to protect their job.

Before injection restarted, three oil division officials chosen by Strickland
conducted a walkthrough of the Bayou with Halff and Citation, according to an
email from Strickland. The rest of the division was left in the dark. That
same day, a pollution abatement manager noted in an email to the commission’s
general counsel that agency critics of the plan had not been invited.

Around the time agency leaders allowed Citation to restart injection in the
Bayou, staff were drafting an extensive contempt case against the company for
rule violations in other parts of the state, according to public records
obtained by The Frontier and ProPublica. Field staff and consultants were
still turning up considerable problems related to Citation’s injection,
including excessive pressures at the sites of destructive eruptions of
wastewater. The staff complaint called for the agency to issue fines and to
terminate well permits. But oil division leaders never signed the paperwork
for the case.

There was ongoing trouble in the Bayou as well. Weeks after Citation restarted
injection, field staff discovered a “severely contaminated” private water well
nearby that had been polluted by oil field waste. Testing showed high levels
of salt as well as the “highest levels of bromide that we have ever sampled,”
according to internal emails, referring to another chemical constituent of oil
and gas waste that poses a public health risk. (The landowners declined to
comment because of an ongoing lawsuit against Citation, but according to court
records, they do not drink from the well. The company, which has fought the
family’s claims, says in a court filing that it has spent hundreds of
thousands of dollars addressing the pollution on their land as part of a plan
approved by the commission.)

By the end of 2024, oil division leaders had allowed six more Citation wells
back online, bringing the total to 13. And the next spring, the agency closed
the Bayou investigation, along with several others related to Citation,
without taking further action.

### Collection of New Complaints

In the year and a half since the Bayou case closed, several of the oil
division staff who had pushed agency leaders to punish Citation have left the
agency, as have a handful of senior leaders. Staffers told The Frontier and
ProPublica they grew frustrated with the agency's unwillingness to crack down
on repeat corporate offenders that agency staff had spent months — at times,
years — investigating.

Tracy Case, an attorney for the oil and gas division, admitted as much at a
national conference for oil regulators in Oklahoma City in May. “I've been
there 11 years doing this and we've never pursued what we call our ‘bad
actors,’” she said, according to a recording of a meeting obtained by the news
outlets. She explained that the oil division is extremely short-staffed while
dealing with hundreds of potential enforcement cases at any one time. An
agency spokesperson declined to comment on behalf of Case.

Less than a third of the roughly 750 enforcement cases filed by the oil
division in the agency’s administrative law courts since 2023 have resulted in
punishment so far, according to a review by The Frontier and ProPublica. The
average fine given out by the agency was about $1,700. The most common
punishment was a $500 fine, combined with using company insurance money to
plug unused wells.  

Neither the Oklahoma Corporation Commission nor Halff responded to questions
about whether the consulting firm still has a role at the state agency.

At the Bayou, nearly all of Citation’s wastewater injection wells are back on,
many operating at pressures beyond Halff’s recommendations. And industry data
indicates that Citation has ramped up oil production to pre-shutdown levels
even as evidence of new purges continues to emerge. In September, fresh layers
of salt — residue of the wastewater — covered the dirt near yellowish puddles
of standing water. Nearby, streaks of oil shone on the ground. The preceding
weeks had been hot and dry, with hardly any rain.

In early October, an agency field staffer requested that Citation install a
specialized well in the Bayou to pump out polluted groundwater, according to a
report in the agency’s incident database.

A slew of new pollution complaints against Citation have continued to appear
in that state database, including more than 60 spills and leaks at well sites
over the past year. Among the complaints were three purges that blew out in
southern Oklahoma over the last three months. All those investigations remain
active, according to state records.  

Another ongoing complaint against Citation originated about 10 miles east of
the Bayou, where a rancher named Mike Faulkner noticed an unusual amount of
salt water gurgling to the surface and flowing down a creek on his land in
April. Nearby, dozens of Citation wells pump wastewater underground.

![A man in a red shirt and cowboy hat holds a small device with its end in a
cup while he stands on muddy ground. ](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_1022_Bowlin_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Rancher
Mike Faulkner measures the water quality on his property in June. Nick
Bowlin/The Frontier

In response, Citation once again blamed the pollution on old drilling
practices, according to an email from one of the company’s engineers to the
Oklahoma Corporation Commission.

Nevertheless, the agency told the company to temporarily shut down some of its
nearby injection wells, and, according to Faulkner, the purge on his land
dried up for the first time in years.

“That tells me that they know the why and the how of that saltwater purging,”
he said in July.

The agency also instructed Citation to install monitoring wells to test for
pollution and to build a pit with a rock dam on Faulkner’s land to catch the
polluted water, along with a fence to keep the cattle out.

![An aerial photo of two trucks parked on grass near an oil well with white
salt covering the area downhill from the well.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/org_5f6dedcca4d18eb7_1781123004000_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Faulkner’s
land was scarred by salt water and contaminated by oil after a Citation well
blew out in June. Courtesy of Mike Faulkner

But in the months since, the agency has given Citation multiple extensions on
the deadline to build the dam and the fencing. In September, Faulkner learned
that the agency granted Citation yet another extension — until December, seven
months after his initial pollution report.

As of October, he said, the wells where the state had asked Citation to pause
operations are injecting — at reduced pressure.

Faulkner said he is fed up with Citation’s yearslong pattern of degrading his
pastures. But he blames state officials for their unwillingness to rein in the
company.

“They're like a spoiled kid,” he said. “They've just gotten away with it for a
long time.”
